Tea grown on the steep hill estates of Darjeeling in West Bengal, India, valued as one of the finest black teas in the world. The first plants were set out in 1841.

The British wanted a source of tea free of Qing China. After the Assam tea plant was found, they also tried the Chinese tea plant. In 1841 Archibald Campbell, the British superintendent at Darjeeling, planted Chinese seeds in his garden there. They throve in the cool, misty climate. Commercial estates followed from the 1850s, helped by Chinese plants and seeds that the botanist Robert Fortune smuggled out of China.

Planters cleared forest and brought in workers, many of them Nepali, whose descendants still pick the leaves by hand. The Darjeeling Himalayan Railway later carried the tea down to the plains. Its light flavour earned it the name "the champagne of teas". In 2004 Darjeeling tea became India's first product with a protected geographical indication, so only tea from listed estates may use the name. It sits beside Assam and Ceylon tea in the story of how tea left China.
